title: Five Talking Points From Man Utd’s Bonkers Eight-Goal Thriller With Aston Villa
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey Whitebloom5:00 PM ESTMatheus Cunha started the first fightback. / Martin Rickett/PA Images/Getty Images“The finest sight in football is Manchester United chasing a game,” the club’s former striker Teddy Sheringham once claimed.
The circumstances which led to the Red Devils finding themselves chasing two separate two-goal deficits against Aston Villa on Sunday wasn’t quite such pleasant viewing for those at Old Trafford.
United are nothing if not entertaining. At this point, each match is its own mini-psychodrama stitched into a wider tapestry of chaos surrounding one of this sport’s great institutions.

Michael Carrick somehow came away from a 4–4 draw salvaged with two stoppage-time goals lamenting how United hadn’t won the game. That was undoubtedly the most favorable interpretation of 98 bonkers minutes.

Michael Carrick captured the mood in Old Trafford. / Sky SportsIt was almost too on the nose. As a deathly hush wrapped around an Old Trafford still trying to figure out how the hosts were trailing 2–0, Carrick was caught by the cameras looking at his wristwatch. Those at Opta had done the counting for the United boss and the numbers were damning.
Villa’s blistering burst had condemned United to their earliest 2–0 deficit in Premier League history with just 220 seconds on the clock.

United failed to even attempt a single pass by the time Alysson had rammed the ball between Senne Lammens’s legs in the 59th second. They only managed one before Nicolas Jackson had doubled the visitors’ advantage—and that was Bruno Fernandes’s kickoff at the restart.

Unai Emery will reflect bitterly on that first half. / Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesThere were plenty of parallels between this contest and United’s Champions League comeback against Roma in midweek. On both occasions, the underwhelming hosts saw the game spin after winning a penalty while trailing 2–0. Fernandes converted at the first time of asking on Sunday and, once more, United’s turnaround thereafter was inspired by the ineptitude of their visitors as much as any injection of ingenuity from Carrick.
Aston Villa, to put it bluntly, started playing like Manchester United.

Youri Tielemans’s first-half equalizer at 2–2 was disastrous from Emery’s point of view. Johan Manzambi and Leon Goretzka both willfully ignored Noussair Mazraoui’s trundle up the right wing, giving the awkward right back enough room to untangle his own feet and pick out a similarly unmarked Tielemans. The only challenge on the former Villa midfielder at the top of the box came from his current teammate, Fernandes.

Villa recovered before the first half’s conclusion and, with Emery’s sharp address still ringing in their ears, rapidly set about steadying themselves to begin the second period. As Villa would discover, United are very capable of beating themselves; you simply have to sit back and let them do it. Villa couldn’t.

Old Trafford was emptying by the time Joshua Zirkzee scored what threatened to be a stoppage-time consolation, finding room in a penalty area crowded with blue and claret shirts who seemed unbothered by the burly Dutchman. Zion Suzuki compounded his side’s collapse with a feeble attempt to punch away a tame corner, sending Unai Emery storming down the tunnel while ripping off his coat as he failed to comprehend quite how Villa hadn’t won that game.

Diogo Dalot has had an interesting week. / Michael Regan/Getty ImagesEarlier this season, the outspoken former Premier League defender Jamie Carragher described “anyone believing Man Utd’s results and performances this season are down to the fact they haven’t got a back-up left back” as “deluded.” In the sense that there are other issues at play, he has a point. But that negligence certainly cost United on Sunday.
It would be charitable to hail Diogo Dalot as a competent right back. His performances on the left don’t inspire the same lukewarm platitudes even at the best of times. These are the worst of times.

Five days on from gifting Matías Soulé the freedom of United’s left flank, Dalot took a similarly dim view of marking Alysson on Sunday, leaving the Brazilian winger bizarrely unattended after closing off his body shape while the ball was rolled past him inside the opening minute.

Even if the fact that Dalot was playing on his wrong side is used as a flimsy defense, that implies that he can’t mirror basic principles he will have lived by his entire senior career, as though he is the soccer equivalent of Ben Stiller’s Derek Zoolander, the dim-witted model who can’t turn left.
Dalot can’t seem to tackle on either side, stabbing a lazy right leg at Alysson who tumbled for a penalty even the Portuguese defender didn’t argue against.

Luke Shaw’s dire injury record hardly makes his current, elongated absence a surprise. Another fitness setback for the similarly fragile Patrick Dorgu has forced Dalot into the entirely predictable role of starting the club’s last four league matches at left back. The failure to secure a competent alternative this summer has repeatedly cost United on the pitch but it’s hardly their only concern, as Carragher—and the club’s fans—would point out.
